label: Shame
framing: Guilt says you did a bad thing. Shame says you are a bad thing. Scripture meets the shamed not with a verdict of disgust but with a covering, a God who makes garments for the exposed and lifts the head that cannot look up.
cultural: The world of the Bible ran on honor and shame, where your standing was your worth and exposure before the group was a kind of social death. The first thing the man and woman did after their fall was hide and sew coverings, and the first thing God did was make better ones, an act of mercy aimed straight at their shame.
historical: The early church preached a crucified Lord, which the Roman world read as the most shameful death imaginable, and called it glory. Augustine in the fourth century traced shame to the rupture between the self we are and the self we display, and the Reformers insisted that the believer's standing rests not on a clean record but on a borrowed righteousness that no exposure can strip away.
application: Bring the hidden thing into the light with one safe person, since shame lives on secrecy and dies in the open. Refuse the lie that your worst moment is your name. Let yourself be covered by grace rather than scrambling to cover yourself, and if old shame has sunk into the body and will not lift, a wise counselor is a gift and not a defeat.

verses.text: And the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked; so they sewed together fig leaves and made coverings for themselves. Then the man and his wife heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the breeze of the day, and they hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden. But the LORD God called out to the man, “Where are you?” “I heard Your voice in the garden,” he replied, “and I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself.”
verses.where: The first thing the man and woman know after they eat is that they are naked, and their first act is to cover themselves and hide. The site's note says their openness to one another is lost first, and that the first fear in Scripture is the terror of a guilty conscience that drives people away from God. God's first word to them is a question that seeks them out: where are you?

verses.text: And the LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and He clothed them.
verses.where: Before he sends them out of the garden, God makes garments of skin and dresses them himself, in place of the fig leaves they had sewn. The site's note says God covers the shame they could not adequately cover themselves, and that the picture of God clothing sinners runs through Scripture. Its plain note asks whether you see God only as the one who sent them out, or also as the one who made their clothes.

verses.text: But You, O LORD, are a shield around me, my glory, and the One who lifts my head.
verses.where: David, fleeing his own son, hears voices saying God will not rescue him, and answers that the LORD is his shield, his glory and the one who lifts his head. The site's plain note says the psalm does not argue with the hardest voice; it turns and speaks to God, and you can make the same turn. A head held down by shame is lifted by another hand.

verses.text: I sought the LORD, and He answered me; He delivered me from all my fears. Those who look to Him are radiant with joy; their faces shall never be ashamed.
verses.where: David says that those who look to the LORD are radiant, their faces never ashamed. By its heading the psalm comes from the time he pretended to be insane in an enemy city, and the site's plain note says thanks can come from humiliating places. The face turned toward God is the one shame cannot keep down.

verses.text: “Do not be afraid,” said David, “for surely I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan. I will restore to you all the land of your grandfather Saul, and you will always eat at my table.” Mephibosheth bowed down and said, “What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog like me?”
verses.where: David looks for anyone left of Saul's house to show kindness for Jonathan's sake, and finds Jonathan's son Mephibosheth, lame in both feet. When David restores his grandfather's land and gives him a lasting place at the king's table, Mephibosheth bows and calls himself a dead dog. The king does not argue with the words; he simply keeps setting his place.

verses.text: Then the woman, seeing that she could not escape notice, came trembling and fell down before Him. In the presence of all the people, she explained why she had touched Him and how she had immediately been healed. “Daughter,” said Jesus, “your faith has healed you. Go in peace.”
verses.where: A woman who had been bleeding for twelve years touches Jesus' cloak, hoping to be healed without being seen. When she cannot stay hidden she comes trembling and tells the whole story in front of everyone, and Jesus calls her daughter. The site's note says the name gives her a family name in public after twelve years on the edges of community life, and its plain note says that by calling her forward Jesus let the crowd see that she was clean.

verses.text: Therefore I tell you, because her many sins have been forgiven, she has loved much. But he who has been forgiven little loves little.” Then Jesus said to her, “Your sins are forgiven.”
verses.where: At a Pharisee's dinner a woman known as a sinner weeps over Jesus' feet, and the host sees only what she has been. Jesus asks him whether he sees this woman, and tells her that her sins are forgiven. The site's plain note says Jesus let her come close when the room wanted her gone, and spoke of her with honour.

verses.text: Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.
verses.where: Hebrews tells weary believers to fix their eyes on Jesus, who for the joy set before him endured the cross, scorning its shame. The cross carried shame as well as pain, and he did not let it name him. The site's plain note asks what it would change today to look at Jesus, who finished the race through shame and pain.

verses.text: Do not be afraid, for you will not be put to shame; do not be intimidated, for you will not be humiliated. For you will forget the shame of your youth and will remember no more the reproach of your widowhood.
verses.where: Zion is pictured as a barren and abandoned wife, and God tells her not to fear, for she will forget the shame of her youth and the reproach of her widowhood. The site's note says her Maker is her husband, who will take her back with everlasting compassion. The shame is not denied; it is outlived.

verses.text: It is just as the Scripture says: “Anyone who believes in Him will never be put to shame.”
verses.where: Paul cites the Scripture: anyone who believes in him will never be put to shame. The site's plain note says the word is near, not a height to climb or a depth to cross, and that anyone can call.

links.label: Practical guides for the inner life

misread.taken: “All our righteous acts are like filthy rags” is quoted to people already full of shame, as if God looked at them and saw only filth, and nothing they are or do could matter to him.
misread.says: The site's note says this verse needs care. It is the prayer of a covenant people confessing that they have sinned and stopped calling on God, and admitting that their religious observances cannot cleanse them while their hearts are turned away. The verse before it says God welcomes those who gladly do right, and two verses later the same people call God their Father and themselves the clay in his hands. Christian traditions draw on the verse in different ways, but on any reading it is a confession the speakers make about themselves, not a verdict on anyone's worth.
misread.text: Each of us has become like something unclean, and all our righteous acts are like filthy rags; we all wither like a leaf, and our iniquities carry us away like the wind.

whole: If shame has turned into hating yourself, or into thoughts of hurting yourself, please tell someone you trust today; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Guilt says you did something wrong. Shame says you are something wrong, and it hides. It replays the moment you were exposed, the thing that was done to you, the habit no one knows about, the family that made you feel like a disappointment from the start. It keeps you from looking people in the eye, and it often keeps you from God, because it is sure he sees what everyone else would see if they knew.

Shame is the first thing Scripture names after the first sin: the man and woman see that they are naked, sew coverings and hide among the trees. The site's note says knowledge gained by disobedience brought shame, not freedom, and that their openness to one another was lost before God even appeared. Shame is not only about what we have done. People carry it for what was done to them, for bodies and families and poverty they never chose, and for weaknesses that are not sins at all. What all of it shares is the conviction that to be seen fully is to be rejected.

Scripture's answer is not to tell the shamed person to stop feeling it, but to show who comes looking. God's first word after the hiding is a question, where are you, and before he sends the couple out he makes them clothes. Jesus calls the woman who hoped to slip away daughter in front of the whole crowd, and lets a woman the room wanted gone come close. So the wisdom here is to stop hiding from the one who already knows: tell him the thing, and tell one safe person, because shame lives on secrecy and loosens in the open. Learn to tell guilt from shame, too. Real wrong can be confessed and forgiven; what was done to you was never yours to confess. And when an old shame will not lift, a wise counselor is a gift, not a defeat.

At the center of the faith is a crucified Lord. Jesus endured the cross, scorning its shame, so no exposure you carry is foreign to him. Mephibosheth called himself a dead dog, and the king kept setting his place at the table. Isaiah promised an abandoned people that they would forget the shame of their youth, and Paul says, “Anyone who believes in Him will never be put to shame.” The last word over you is not the thing you most fear someone will find out. It is the name he calls you by.
deep.sit: What is the thing you are most afraid someone will find out, and what would it mean to hear God's question, where are you, as the voice of one coming to clothe you rather than to expose you?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note asks what you would like God to forget, and says the psalm lets you ask: he remembers you according to his loving devotion, not according to your past.
prayer.text: To You, O LORD, I lift up my soul; in You, my God, I trust. Do not let me be put to shame; do not let my enemies exult over me. Surely none who wait for You will be put to shame; but those who are faithless without cause will be disgraced. Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my rebellious acts; remember me according to Your loving devotion, because of Your goodness, O LORD.

careLines.text: If what happened to you was not your choice, it is not your sin, and you deserve safety and help from someone you trust.
You do not have to pretend you are fine.
Tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor or a friend.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
